title: US Appeals Court Denies Constitutional Bond Hearings for Detained Migrants
excerpt: The 5th Circuit ruled 10-7 that the Fifth Amendment does not require bond hearings for detained immigrants, reversing a July ruling and affecting Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi.
body:
• The 5th US Circuit Court of Appeals ruled 10-7 on October 23 that detained immigrants who entered the US illegally have no constitutional right to a bond hearing, reversing a July panel ruling that required a hearing after 90 days.
  • The ruling applies in Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi, the states under the 5th Circuit, which together hold the largest numbers of immigration detainees in the country.
  • The Supreme Court has agreed to hear a related case this term, but only on whether federal statute requires bond hearings, not on the constitutional question decided here.
  • If you or a family member is detained in Texas, Louisiana or Mississippi, a constitutional claim alone will no longer secure a bond hearing there; detainees can still request a bond redetermination from an immigration judge under the Executive Office for Immigration Review process, with no filing fee, and should seek legal counsel on statutory and habeas options.

A US appeals court ruled on Friday, October 23, that the Trump administration is not required under the US Constitution to give detained immigrants a chance to seek release on bond. In a 10-7 ruling, the New Orleans-based 5th US Circuit Court of Appeals held that the Fifth Amendment's due process protections do not require immigration detainees to receive bond hearings, according to Reuters.

The decision reverses a July ruling by a 2-1 panel of the same court, which had held that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement could not constitutionally detain people for more than 90 days without providing hearings to argue for release on bond.

What the majority held

US Circuit Judge Cory Wilson, a Trump appointee, wrote the majority opinion. The court concluded that detained immigrants are not constitutionally entitled to proceedings in immigration court beyond what Congress has provided by statute.

https://x.com/DiamondandSilk/status/2114049045878448256

"To the extent petitioners seek to vindicate a liberty interest to be free from physical restraint in the most abstract sense, they can do so at any moment by agreeing to leave the country."

— US Circuit Judge Cory Wilson

The cases were brought by two Mexican citizens and one Honduran, according to Reuters. The three men had lived in the United States for roughly 14 to 22 years and were detained after traffic stops.

The full court agreed to rehear the case after the July panel decision and reversed course. In February, the 5th Circuit had adopted the administration's reading of immigration law as requiring mandatory detention.

Why Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi matter

The ruling carries particular weight because Texas and Louisiana house the nation's largest numbers of immigration detainees, and the 5th Circuit's jurisdiction also covers Mississippi. If left to stand, the decision would eliminate a key avenue for detained migrants in those three states to argue for release, especially if the Supreme Court decides the administration's detention practice complies with immigration law.

Judge Dana Douglas, an appointee of President Joe Biden, was among the dissenting judges.

"Unchecked, executive authority to arrest and detain, indefinitely, echoes fearfully from history."

— US Circuit Judge Dana Douglas, dissenting

Ellie Norton, a lawyer for the non-US citizens in the case at the National Immigration Project, said in a statement: "This ruling opens the door to more people being locked up for no reason, with devastating consequences for them, their loved ones and their community." James Percival, general counsel for the US Department of Homeland Security, hailed the result in a social media post as a "big win in the 5th Circuit on mandatory detention for illegal aliens," according to Reuters.

How bond hearings normally work

Under the Executive Office for Immigration Review's bond proceedings guidance, bond is initially set by the Department of Homeland Security, and an immigration judge may conduct a bond hearing to redetermine the amount on request. A request can be made in writing or orally in court, should state the person's full name, alien registration number and detention location, and carries no filing fee. The US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, based in New Orleans, is the appellate court for federal districts in Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi.

What happens next

The Supreme Court this month agreed to consider the related detention issue, which has divided lower courts. Numerous lawsuits by migrants arguing they were unlawfully detained have reached the courts as ICE implemented the administration's deportation agenda, according to Reuters. The Supreme Court is considering only whether such hearings are required by statute, not by the Constitution, which was the issue the 5th Circuit addressed on Friday.

For diaspora families in Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi, detention is now harder to challenge on constitutional grounds alone. Families should record the detention location and A-number, request any available bond redetermination promptly, and get counsel to assess statutory or habeas claims ahead of the Supreme Court's decision.
